title: Perform primary meat inspection incisions of game

lessons.title: Game harvesting and preparing for inspection
lessons.html:
Game meat in South Africa

Game meat (venison) from species such as springbok, blesbok, impala, kudu, black wildebeest and gemsbok is an important product of South African game farms, both locally and for export. Unlike domestic stock, most game is not inspected alive at an abattoir. Animals are usually harvested in the field by shooting, then bled and eviscerated in the field or at a field depot, and transported to a registered game abattoir or game handling facility for inspection under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations.

What this means for inspection

  • No normal ante-mortem inspection. The hunter or the trained person at harvest must observe the animals before shooting and record abnormal behaviour or condition. These records travel with the carcass.
  • Time and temperature: delays between shooting, bleeding, evisceration and cooling increase spoilage. The times are recorded.
  • Organs: the pluck and viscera may need to accompany the carcass, identified with the same number, as the regulations and the facility require.

Preparing the station

  • Good lighting, a clean rail, sterilizer, hand-wash basin, two sharp knives, steel and hook.
  • System to match carcasses, organs and harvest records.
  • Detention area, tags, condemned containers and sample containers.
  • PPE.

Planning

  1. Check harvest records: species, number, farm, date and time of shooting, evisceration and arrival.
  2. Check for notes on abnormal behaviour or condition before shooting.
  3. Know which diseases are present in the region, for example tuberculosis or anthrax in certain areas, and follow any veterinary controls in force.

lessons.title: Performing the incisions on game carcasses
lessons.html:
Routine examination

Game antelope are ruminants, so inspection follows a routine similar to cattle or small stock, depending on body size, as set out in the regulations and your training.

Shot wound and carcass

  • Find and examine the bullet wound and its path. A head or neck shot gives the least meat damage. Body shots cause haemorrhage and bone fragments; gut shots contaminate the body cavity with ingesta.
  • Trim the shot area and bullet path to remove damaged, bloody tissue and possible lead fragments.
  • Observe the carcass for bruising (especially in animals that were captured or chased), old injuries, abscesses, emaciation, oedema and contamination with hair, soil and ingesta.
  • Check the colour and smell of the meat and the condition of the body cavity: delayed evisceration gives a green discolouration and bad smell.

Head

  • Observe the head and incise the head lymph nodes and masseter muscles as prescribed for the species, looking for abscesses, tuberculous lesions and measles cysts.

Pluck and viscera (when present)

  • Lungs: observe and palpate; incise the bronchial and mediastinal nodes. Look for lungworm, hydatid cysts, pneumonia and tuberculous lesions.
  • Heart: examine and incise as prescribed for measles cysts.
  • Liver: observe, palpate and incise the bile ducts for liver fluke; look for cysts and abscesses.
  • Observe the stomachs, intestines and spleen; an enlarged, dark spleen and dark, non-clotting blood may indicate anthrax: stop and refer at once without further cutting.

Muscles

Look for Sarcocystis cysts, which can appear as white streaks in muscle in some game species, and for measles cysts.

Hygiene

Sterilise after every carcass and after cutting into lesions. Do not let carcasses touch the floor or each other.

lessons.title: Completing the game inspection
lessons.html:
Findings and actions

FindingAction
Normal carcass, clean head or neck shotTrim shot area; continue to marking
Gut shot with contamination of the body cavityTrim extensively; detain and refer if contamination is widespread
Delayed evisceration with green discolouration and bad smellDetain and refer; may be condemned
Localised abscess or bruiseMark for trimming
Liver fluke or cysts in one organCondemn the organ
Tuberculous lesionsDetain and refer; report as required
Signs suggesting anthraxStop, do not cut further, detain and report immediately

Records

  • Species, carcass number, farm of origin and harvest records.
  • Times of shooting, evisceration and arrival, and chilling details.
  • Findings, trimming, condemnations and detentions.
  • Samples taken and results.

Export markets often require full traceability back to the farm and the harvest event.

Feedback

  • To the harvesting team: poor shot placement, delayed evisceration, dirty handling or slow cooling.
  • To the farm: parasite levels, condition of animals, disease findings.

Safety

Game can carry zoonoses such as tuberculosis and anthrax. Wear PPE, cover cuts, sterilise instruments, and report any illness.

Key points

  • Game is usually field-harvested, so harvest records replace normal ante-mortem inspection.
  • Examine and trim the shot wound and bullet path.
  • Gut shots and delayed evisceration cause contamination and spoilage.
  • Follow a ruminant inspection routine for head, pluck, liver and carcass.
  • Suspected anthrax: stop, do not cut further, and report immediately.
